citation: Fraichard, T. & Asama, H. (2004). "Inevitable Collision States: a step towards safer robots." Advanced Robotics 18(10), 1001-1024.

derivation.human: Treat the far side of every occlusion boundary as potentially occupied, so the effective free distance is the distance to the boundary rather than to the nearest return. The speed cap then binds BEFORE anything is visible, which is the whole difference from the dynamic-window form: rounding the blind corner at (6, 5) the robot slows on approach to the corner rather than on first sight of what is behind it.
derivation.model: Model the Go2 under the frozen policy as a bounded-acceleration unicycle in the body frame: state (x, y, theta, vx, vy, wz), control the Twist. Before emitting any candidate Twist u, evaluate the state it will produce after one control interval, s' = f(s, u, tau), and test s' against a finite evasive manoeuvre set E — the paper's conservative subset. Take E to be three braking manoeuvres: brake straight, brake while turning at +wz_max, brake while turning at -wz_max, each decelerating at a_max until rest. Roll each manoeuvre forward in the body frame from s' and sweep the robot footprint (inflated by the collision radius) along it. If *every* manoeuvre in E intersects an obstacle, s' is declared ICS and u is vetoed; the node then emits the best surviving candidate, falling back to the pure braking Twist (0, 0, 0) if none survives. Obstacles come from the 181-beam scan in the current body frame only, which sidesteps odometry drift: the check is re-run every cycle from fresh range data, so a drifting pose estimate cannot corrupt it. My numbers, not the paper's: a_max = 1.0 m/s^2, tau = 0.2 s actuation-plus-latency interval (so braking distance vx^2/(2*a_max) + vx*tau), inflation radius 0.35 m, wz_max = 1.0 rad/s. Extension beyond this paper, flagged as such: beams at or past max range and the two angular sectors the 181-beam scan does not cover are treated as *occupied* at the range limit, so unseen space cannot be mistaken for a valid escape corridor. That closure is not in Fraichard & Asama 2004 and is the part of this card most in need of independent support.

mechanism.human: An inevitable collision state is one from which a collision occurs for ANY future sequence of controls. Safety is therefore a property of the state the robot is entering, not of the obstacles it can currently see - and a bound computed only against visible obstacles is unsound wherever the world is occluded.
mechanism.model: A state is an Inevitable Collision State (ICS) if, no matter what control trajectory the system applies from that state onward, a collision with an obstacle eventually occurs. The key claim is that collision-freeness of the current state is not a safety property: a robot can be arbitrarily far from every obstacle and still be doomed, because its dynamics and bounded deceleration make the collision unavoidable over the infinite horizon. Safety therefore has to be a property of the *state* (pose plus velocity) evaluated against the *future* trajectory set, not of the instantaneous clearance. The paper shows ICS is characterised by intersecting over the set of possible future trajectories and unioning over the obstacles, and proves the property that makes this usable online: evaluating the intersection over a *subset* of future trajectories yields a superset of the true ICS set. Checking only a few evasive manoeuvres is therefore conservative — it may refuse a state that was actually salvageable, but it never certifies a doomed state as safe. This helps because it converts an infinite-horizon guarantee into a finite, cheap-to-evaluate test, and it makes the finite manoeuvre set a tunable safety/permissiveness dial rather than a heuristic.

trigger.human: An occlusion boundary - a depth discontinuity in the scan - lies within the distance the robot would need to stop from its current speed.
trigger.model: Applies whenever a command is about to be committed for a control interval to a system with bounded deceleration, non-zero current velocity, and a sensing horizon shorter than its stopping distance. On the Go2 all three hold: the frozen locomotion policy cannot stop instantly, commanded speed is non-negligible, and the planar lidar sees a bounded range with blind sectors. It does not apply at rest with a verified-clear braking envelope, where the zero-velocity state is trivially non-ICS.
